title: The Operationalization of “Fields” as WoS Subject Categories (WCs) in Evaluative Bibliometrics: The cases of “Library and Information Science” and “Science & Technology Studies”
venue: Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in evaluative bibliometrics: whether Web of Science Subject Categories (WCs) are sufficiently precise and valid for normalizing citation impact across fields. The authors argue that WCs, although widely treated as a “best practice” for defining reference sets in bibliometric evaluation, were originally created for information retrieval and have evolved incrementally, which can produce indexer effects and blur analytical distinctions between fields.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or human participants. Instead, it examines bibliometric classification practices using two empirical examples from scholarly publishing: library and information science (LIS), which is assigned a WC, and science and technology studies (STS), which is not cleanly represented by a single WC. The authors analyze journal-journal citation structures, WC assignments, and category overlaps to show how journals within LIS split into substructures and how STS journals span multiple unrelated WCs, making normalization difficult or misleading.

The main conclusion is that WoS subject categories are too crude for detailed evaluative purposes, especially for interdisciplinary areas, and may seriously distort comparisons if used for field-normalized citation indicators. The authors suggest that alternatives such as Scopus-based classifications, custom journal schemes, paper-level subject indexing (e.g., MeSH), audience-based reference sets, or algorithmic clustering may offer better options, though each has limitations. Overall, the paper is a theoretical and methodological critique of field normalization practices rather than an empirical study of instructional technology or learning outcomes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a bibliometric methodology/opinion paper about journal classification and citation normalization, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It does not present K-12 learning-outcome data, an experimental design, or implementation evidence relevant to Khanmigo or any other AI tutoring system.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact on student learning outcomes or educational operations; its contribution is conceptual and confined to evaluative bibliometrics. It does not evaluate technology use in classrooms or report any measurable educational effects.
